node.label: Quentin Skinner
node.date_label: Meaning and Understanding in the History of Ideas (1969) · The Foundations of Modern Political Thought (1978) · Liberty before Liberalism: inaugural lecture (1997) · Liberty before Liberalism: extended published essay (1998) · On Encountering the Past: interview with Koikkalainen and Syrjämäki (2002)
node.description: A historian of political thought who asks what historically situated writers were doing with their words. His 1969 argument treats public conventions and possible interventions as evidence against reading timeless doctrines out of classic texts. His later first-person account credits Collingwood, Wittgenstein and analytical philosophy while warning against tidy intellectual autobiography. Liberty before Liberalism states a program of recovering a neo-Roman account of civil liberty displaced by liberal predominance. Contextual inquiry is itself contested: Pocock’s 1996 discussion singles out Skinner’s search for the modern state as vulnerable to imposing later categories on earlier actors.
node.representative_figures_and_works: “Meaning and Understanding in the History of Ideas” (1969); The Foundations of Modern Political Thought (1978, unread here; particular criticism mediated by Pocock); Liberty before Liberalism (lecture 12 November 1997; extended book 1998, preface and pp. 1–4 read); “On Encountering the Past” (2002 interview with Petri Koikkalainen and Sami Syrjämäki).
node.scope_note: No complete career review or whole-book reading. Prior source qualifications remain. Fresh 2026-10-24 reading: 1969 article pp. 37–38 and 50–52; 2002 manuscript answers 1 and 6; Liberty before Liberalism preface ix–xiv and printed pp. 1–4, with the publisher copyright leaf distinguishing first publication 1998 from lecture 1997 and Canto reissue 2012; Pocock’s published 1996 criticism at pp. 54–55. The original Collingwood passage remains uncollated. Skinner’s retrospective recollection is explicit reception evidence, not a shared method of every Cambridge historian. Collective edges that also name Dunn, Pocock or Brett stay on the group entry; only claims specifically about Skinner move to his individual endpoint.

proposed_edges.relationship: Makes the historically possible intervention, rather than a timeless doctrine, central to interpreting political texts; recalls that public uses and intentions guided his practice (1969; retrospective interview 2002).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: 1969 pp. 37–38, 50–52 and 2002 answers 1/6 reread, with the earlier wider reading scope retained. This is his individual methodological contribution to the contextual field. The reception arrows for Wittgenstein and Collingwood keep their old IDs; aggregate edges also naming Dunn, Pocock and Brett are not reassigned to him.

proposed_edges.relationship: Uses the history of early modern liberty and sovereignty to reopen alternatives to the later predominance of liberal accounts of civil liberty (Liberty before Liberalism, 1998).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: The author’s preface ix–xiv states the recovery program; chapter opening pp. 1–4 treats rival accounts of sovereignty in the English Civil War. This is an attributed statement of his project, not a claim to have read or independently verified the full book or a single doctrine shared by all political historians.
